articles.title: Who Killed Asylum?
articles.author: Levi Vonk
articles.content_excerpt: Asylum as we know it is basically dead. The immigration system has been so systematically hollowed out that, for the vast majority of the world’s poor and displaced, it might as well not exist anymore. A brief list of what’s gone wrong: First, asylum approval rates have plummeted to historic lows, falling below 20 percent in 2025, compared to 55.5 percent in 2012. Second, the process is slower than ever before. A backlog of over three million cases frequently forces potential asylees to wait five or more years before finally appearing in court. In 2012, there were only about 300,000 cases on the docket, less than one-tenth of today’s, and wait times of just a year and a half . This backlog has led to a third problem. articles.title: The United Arab Emirates Is Devastating Sudan for Profit
articles.author: Husam Mahjoub
articles.content_excerpt: At one time or another, Sudanese governments have hosted, armed, or tolerated rebels and opposition groups from all of the country’s neighbors, from Egypt and Libya to Uganda and Ethiopia. Sudan’s neighbors have repaid the favor, and a range of outside actors are now involved in the Sudanese civil war. Key supporters of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) include Chad, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and South Sudan. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Eritrea support the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the de facto government. Among all the external actors, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is the most consequential, even though it has the least reason to be involved. articles.title: We Can’t Blame the Supreme Court for Congress’s Problems
articles.author: Harry Blain
articles.content_excerpt: Almost everyone on the Left seems to have lost faith in the Supreme Court of the United States. This would have been improbable in 1954, after the Brown v. Board of Education decision, or in 1973, after Roe v. Wade , or even in 1992, after the court upheld the core holding of Roe in Planned Parenthood v. Casey . But after over twenty years of the conservative John Roberts serving as chief justice, including over half a decade of him leading a court with a 6–3 conservative supermajority, liberals and progressives no longer turn to the court with any real hope. If anything, they view it with hostility. articles.title: In Italy’s Financial Capital, Socialism Is Back in the Air
articles.author: Jacopo Custodi
articles.content_excerpt: One in twelve people living in Milan is a millionaire. A report by the consultancy Henley & Partners ranks Italy’s second-largest city and financial capital as the world leader for millionaires per resident, well ahead of New York City, where the figure is one in twenty-two. A growing number come from abroad, drawn not just by the vibrancy of Italy’s fashion hub but also generous tax breaks for wealthy newcomers. For everyone else, Milan tells a very different story. The cost of living is soaring, and with rents and house prices spiraling out of control, working people are being pushed to the suburbs.
